This lab has exercises that reinforce the sections "Finding and stopping a process" and "Background job administration" of Lecture 2 (`lectures/lec02_linux_advanced.qmd`). Everything is done at the **terminal** (not by clicking in a file browser). You will need to open a second terminal in a few places. In Part 5 you also need `tmux`: `sudo apt install tmux` on Ubuntu or `brew install tmux` on a Mac.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Ground rules
* Run every command yourself. Many answers depend on what you see on your own machine (and your PID numbers will not be the same as anyone else's).
* Leave the "#TODO text [question text] text" line and start a new line underneath and write your answers on that new line
* Clean up after yourself. Every part ends by stopping the processes it started. Check with `pgrep -a sleep` that none are left over.
:::

# Part 1: Looking at processes with `ps` and `pgrep`

`sleep 600` does nothing for 10 minutes, which makes it a perfect process to look at. The `&` at the end runs it in the **background**, so you get your prompt back. The shell stores the PID of the last background process in the variable `$!`:

```bash
sleep 600 &
echo $!
```

```bash
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,command -p $!
```

# Part 3: Signals and `kill`

`kill` sends a **signal** to a process. In Lab 2 you saw that a process killed by signal number *n* has exit status 128 + *n*. List all of the signals and find the numbers of `HUP`, `INT`, `KILL`, `TERM`, `STOP` and `CONT`:

```bash
kill -l
```

Create a program that refuses to die when it is politely asked to stop. The `trap '' TERM` line tells bash to ignore the TERM signal:

```bash
cat > stubborn.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
trap '' TERM
while true; do sleep 1; done
EOF
chmod +x stubborn.sh
./stubborn.sh &
echo $!
```

Ask it to stop (the default signal of `kill` is TERM) and look at it:

```bash
kill $!
sleep 2
ps -o pid,stat,command -p $!
```

#TODO [is the process still there, and why? <1pts>]
#TODO [write the command that stops it for sure, and the command that proves that it is gone <1pts>]

Use `wait` to get the exit status of processes that were killed by different signals. `wait PID` waits for that process and then sets `$?` to its exit status:

```bash
sleep 600 &
kill $!
wait $!
echo $?

sleep 600 &
kill -9 $!
wait $!
echo $?
```

#TODO [the two exit statuses that you got, and which signal numbers do they correspond to? <2pts>]

A process can be paused without dying. `STOP` suspends it and `CONT` resumes it. This is the signal that Ctrl+Z sends (almost; Ctrl+Z sends a variant called `TSTP`):

```bash
sleep 600 &
kill -STOP $!
ps -o pid,stat,command -p $!
kill -CONT $!
ps -o pid,stat,command -p $!
kill $!
```

#TODO [what was the `STAT` in each of the two `ps` lines? <1pts>]

There is also `pkill`, which kills by *name* instead of by PID. Without running it, think about this one:

```bash

```

# Part 4: Surviving a logout with `nohup`

When you close a terminal, the system sends the **HUP** ("hang-up") signal to the programs that were started from it, and by default they die. `nohup` makes a program ignore HUP. You can test that without closing anything, by sending HUP yourself:

```bash
sleep 600 &
echo $!
nohup sleep 601 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
echo $!
```

#TODO [what does `> /dev/null 2>&1` do, and why does `nohup` need it in this line? <1pts>]

Send the HUP signal to both processes and see which ones survive. Use `wait` on the first one to see its exit status:

```bash
#TODO [command that sends HUP to the two sleeps you just started <1pts>]
pgrep -a sleep
```

Clean up what is left:

```bash
kill $(pgrep -x sleep)
```

Now a realistic job. This script is a stand-in for a long computation: it writes the date to the standard output every second.

```bash
cat > infinite_loop.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while true; do date; sleep 1; done
EOF
chmod +x infinite_loop.sh
```

# Part 5: A terminal that survives: `tmux`

`nohup` keeps one command alive. `tmux` keeps a whole **terminal** alive, so that you can go away and come back to see it as you left it. Start a session called `lab3`:

```bash
tmux new -s lab3
```

You are now inside tmux (note the green bar at the bottom). Inside it, start the loop in the background and look at it:

```bash
cd $HOME/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/labs/03/scratch   # edit if your repo is elsewhere
./infinite_loop.sh > out.log 2>&1 &
tail -n 2 out.log
```

Detach: press Ctrl+B, release both keys, then press d. You are back in your normal terminal. Look at the session and at the job, and then come back:

```bash
tmux ls
ps aux | grep "[i]nfinite_loop"
jobs
tmux attach -t lab3
jobs
```

#TODO [paste the line that `tmux ls` printed. Why did `jobs` print nothing in the normal terminal but print the job after you attached? <1pts>]

Inside the session, press Ctrl+B and then c to create a second tabbed window, and Ctrl+B and then n / p to move between the two. Then detach again and kill the whole session from outside:

```bash
tmux kill-session -t lab3
tmux ls
ps aux | grep "[i]nfinite_loop"
```

#TODO [is the loop still running after the session was killed? Explain what you saw in one sentence using what you learned about HUP in Part 4. <2pts>]

You do not have to attach to a session to start something in it. The `-d` option starts a session **detached** and runs a command in it:

```bash
#TODO [one line command that creates a detached tmux session called lab3b which runs infinite_loop.sh and writes its output to out.log <2pts>]
tmux ls
tail -n 2 out.log
ps aux | grep "[i]nfinite_loop"
```

```bash

ps aux | grep "[i]nfinite_loop"
```
